newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Power makes S.Africa a world-class aluminium site.
newsitem.headline: Power makes S.Africa a world-class aluminium site.

text.p: South Africa will remain a world-class location for primary aluminium smelting provided power utilities continue to offer low-cost electricity, Resource Strategies Inc president Robin Adams said on Monday.
Adams told a Metal Bulletin mining and metals conference that South Africa had emerged over the past couple of years as desirable location for power-intensive industries.
He said Africa, with its mineral resources and power generation potential, held a comparable strategic position to the Commonwealth of Independent States.

"When this (electricity and gas) resource base is coupled with the mineral deposits of the region, we have an overall strategic position here that is arguably the equal of that in the CIS but is much closer to deepwater and above all, far more stable from the political perspective," Adams said.
He said South Africa would continue to remain a prime location for primary aluminium smelting.
Referring to Gencor Ltd's Alusaf smelter at Richards Bay -- one of the lowest cost aluminium producers in the world -- Adams said the price of Alusaf's power was tied to the LME price of aluminium.

"I somehow doubt that the next aluminium smelter will be constructed on the same type of deal as Hillside. The power supply will be guaranteed for 20 to 30 years, but the terms of sale are likely to be reset to market conditions at periodic intervals," Adams said.
"The notion that power prices can be indexed to measures of general inflation for the purpose of long-term contracts will no longer be acceptable to aluminium companies in our opinion," he added.
Alusaf's new Hillside smelter was fully commissioned in June this year and continues to run well above design capacity.
Production is currently 495,000 tonnes a year at Hillside -- designed to produce 466,000 tonnes of aluminium a year.
Adams said a commodity market in electricity was emerging where producers and consumers could fix prices for several years ahead and hedge the risks in a similiar manner to commodity metal markets.
"Once the electricity market develops depth and liquidity, aluminium smelters will be able to design their own risk-sharing tariffs through simultaneous forward transactions in metal and power.
"They will not need to have an utility on the other side of these deals anymore than a producer needs a specific consumer on the other side of a forward metal sale," he said.
